title: Keeping Up With Science #3: Space Exploration & Commercializing Mars

teacherNotes.title: Lesson Stage Aims
teacherNotes.content: Examine space economy, public space agencies vs private aerospace firms (NASA vs SpaceX), extraterrestrial resource mining, and Mars colonization.

elements.content: Discuss the following questions with your partner (3-4 minutes):

1. If offered a seat on a one-way mission to establish a permanent colony on Mars, would you accept?
2. Is spending billions on space travel justified when Earth faces severe environmental and social challenges?
3. How do you view space tourism for wealthy private citizens?
Study key terms in astrophysics and space economics:

1. Terraforming (/ˈter.ə.fɔː.mɪŋ/): Hypothetical engineering process of altering a planet's atmosphere and temperature to make it habitable for Earth life.
   • Example: 'Terraforming Mars would require thickening its thin atmosphere with greenhouse gases.'

2. Commercial Aerospace (/kəˈmɜː.ʃəl ˈeə.rəʊ.speɪs/): Private business sector engaged in designing, launching, and operating spacecraft.
   • Example: 'The rise of commercial aerospace has significantly reduced launch costs per kilogram.'

3. Asteroid Mining (/ˈæs.tər.ɔɪd ˈmaɪ.nɪŋ/): The exploitation of raw materials from asteroids and small planets.
   • Example: 'Asteroid mining could unlock vast reserves of rare metals like platinum and cobalt.'

4. Extraterrestrial Settlement (/ˌek.strə.təˈres.tri.əl ˈset.əl.mənt/): Permanent human colonies established beyond Earth.
   • Example: 'Building a self-sustaining extraterrestrial settlement requires closed-loop life support systems.'

slides.title: Reading: Public Exploration vs Private Enterprise

elements.content: Read the passage and complete the comprehension check:

'Historically, space exploration was the exclusive domain of sovereign governments driven by national prestige. Today, reusable rocket technology pioneered by private corporations has altered space economics. Lower launch costs enable ambitious commercial ventures ranging from satellite internet constellations to lunar resource extraction. However, international space law, codified in the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, lacks clear enforcement rules regarding property rights and commercial exploitation beyond Earth.'
What challenge does the passage highlight regarding commercial space activities?
options: Reusable rockets have increased the cost of launching satellites.
Government space agencies have banned private corporations from launching rockets.
International space law lacks clear enforcement mechanisms for property rights.
Asteroids do not contain valuable metals or water ice.
answers: International space law lacks clear enforcement mechanisms for property rights.

elements.content: Useful phrases for debate on public spending and scientific priorities:

• 'From an economic feasibility standpoint...'
• 'While space exploration yields indirect technological spinoffs, others argue...'
• 'How do we prioritize planetary stewardship vs space expansion?'
• 'It is imperative that international treaties keep pace with...'

1. Is establishing a multi-planetary human species necessary to protect humanity from potential extinction events?
2. Should a Mars colony be governed by Earth nations or develop its own independent laws and political system?
3. What psychological challenges might early Mars settlers experience living in isolated enclosed habitats?

slides.title: Discussion Round 2: Space Debris & Environmental Impact

elements.content:
Thousands of inactive satellites and orbital debris encircle Earth ('Kessler Syndrome').
• Who should pay to clean up space junk in Earth's orbit?
• Are we at risk of polluting other planets before we even colonize them?

• Role A (Space Agency Director): Requests $50B for a lunar base, citing technological spinoffs (solar tech, water filtration, GPS).
• Role B (Environmental Advocate): Demands redirecting $50B to terrestrial carbon capture and reforestation projects.
Live feedback notes on vocabulary, pronunciation, and accuracy:
